clue.text: No trumpery throwaways, these

parts.note: in bridge, cards thrown away on a trick when a player cannot follow suit, which are not trumps

explanation.surface: Something dismissed as worthless rubbish, nothing showy about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trumpery' looks like the old word for showy rubbish, but here it means 'of trumps': cards a bridge player throws away without trumping.
explanation.definitionFit: Cards thrown away in a card game are the hand's rejects, and they are not trumps.

clue.text: Just begun with short measure cereal, note

parts.note: an inch is a small unit of length
oats are a cereal crop
E is a note of the musical scale

explanation.surface: Breakfast has barely started: a little cereal, and a reminder note.
explanation.definitionFit: Something inchoate is only just started and not yet fully formed, rudimentary.

clue.text: One not "handled" in the field?

parts.note: a knight dubbed at court, kneeling on a carpet, rather than for deeds done on the field of battle

explanation.surface: A player who never touched the ball out on the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'field' is a battlefield, not a sports field: a knight given the title for service at home, never tested in war, is sneered at as one who knelt on carpet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an old sneer for a stay-at-home soldier knighted for civil service rather than military valour.

clue.text: Darling girl. Stout lad. To name but two

definitions.text: Darling girl. Stout lad. To name but two

parts.words: Darling girl. Stout lad. To name but two
parts.note: Grace Darling famously rowed out to save shipwrecked sailors in 1838; a stout-hearted lad is another such lifesaver

explanation.surface: A fond list of a sweet girl and a plump boy.
explanation.walkthrough: Grace Darling, a lighthouse keeper's daughter, became a British heroine for saving shipwreck survivors; 'Darling' and 'Stout' look like terms of endearment and description but name a heroine and a brave quality.
explanation.definitionFit: Lifesavers are people who save others from danger, as Grace Darling did.

clue.text: He waits on board, to make enquiry of course

definitions.meaning: a ship's attendant serves passengers on board
racecourse officials hold an enquiry into a race when the result is disputed

explanation.walkthrough: 'Of course' looks like 'naturally' but means 'of the racecourse', where officials hold a stewards' enquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's attendant serves passengers, and the officials who police horse racing hold enquiries at the course.

clue.text: A crime to reform a kingdom ?

indicators.note: reforming the words a crime remakes them, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A call to reform criminals as a way of building a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: This was one of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms of central England.

clue.text: Less than a pint means a breather for some drinkers

definitions.meaning: a measure of a quarter of a pint
fish, which live in water, breathe through this organ

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drinkers' look like pub-goers taking a pause, but are fish, which 'drink like a fish'; a breather is their breathing organ.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a small liquid measure and the organ through which fish take oxygen from water.

clue.text: Like Botticelli's Venus, with or without the tail

definitions.text: Like Botticelli's Venus, with or without the tail

parts.words: Like Botticelli's Venus, with or without the tail
parts.note: the painting shows the goddess risen from the ocean on a shell; the word may be spelt with or without a final E

explanation.surface: An art critic describing the famous goddess, perhaps as a mermaid.
explanation.walkthrough: In Botticelli's The Birth of Venus the goddess arrives from the waves; 'tail' looks like a mermaid's but is the optional last letter E.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus was born from the foam of the ocean, so she came from or was carried by the waves.

clue.text: Monograph on the soundness of international agreements

indicators.note: the sound of the words is what counts, so a word that sounds like the next piece is wanted

parts.note: treaties are agreements between nations

explanation.surface: A scholarly paper judging whether international pacts are sound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundness' looks like reliability but signals a homophone.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal written study of a single subject is a scholarly essay of that kind.

clue.text: Mark of 13 perhaps on the mountain-side

definitions.meaning: 13 across is BATTLE, and a wound mark from fighting is the kind meant
a steep rocky cliff on a hillside

explanation.walkthrough: 13 refers to the answer at 13 across, a fight that leaves its mark on a soldier's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both the mark a healed wound leaves and a craggy cliff face on a hill.

clue.text: P.C papers were posthumous

parts.note: Dickens's first novel was titled The Posthumous Papers of a club whose initials are P.C.

explanation.surface: A police officer's documents were published after his death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'P.C' looks like a police constable, but stands for the club in the full title of Dickens's novel, The Posthumous Papers of the Pickwick Club.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens named Mr Pickwick's society in his novel's full title as the subject of the posthumous papers.

clue.text: His clients' lands held great ones, claimed Brown

definitions.text: His clients' lands held great ones, claimed Brown

parts.words: His clients' lands held great ones, claimed Brown
parts.note: the 18th-century garden designer Lancelot Brown told landowners their estates had great potential, which earned him his nickname

explanation.surface: An estate agent named Brown boasts of his clients' fine properties.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancelot 'Capability' Brown, the English landscape gardener, was nicknamed for telling clients their grounds had great potential for improvement.
explanation.definitionFit: Potentials or latent qualities are what Brown claimed every estate possessed.

clue.text: In which this bold soldier lost his legs

definitions.text: In which this bold soldier lost his legs

parts.words: In which this bold soldier lost his legs
parts.note: Thomas Hood's comic poem Faithless Nelly Gray begins with Ben, a soldier bold, whose legs were shot off in war

explanation.surface: A war story about a brave soldier who was maimed.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does two jobs: the hero of Hood's poem is surnamed for this fight, and a cannon-ball in a fight took off his legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight between armies is where the poem's soldier lost his legs, and it is also his surname.

clue.text: Make second entrance, like fruit after mutation

indicators.note: a mutation changes form, so the letters are rearranged
a like fruit means another of the same kind, so the fruit is taken twice

parts.note: a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A fruit that comes back again after a genetic change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like fruit' gives PEAR and a like one, PEARPEAR, which 'after mutation' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: To come back onto the stage or into view is to show up once more.

clue.text: Extremely poor in Anglo- French Middle East

parts.note: in English, mean means middle or average
est is the French word for east

explanation.surface: Dire poverty found in a Middle East country with British and French ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anglo-French' says to take 'Middle' in English and 'East' in French.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of mean, poor or shabby: the most wretched and stingy.

clue.text: Cheeky monkey's got right into the brewer's grain

indicators.note: one piece has made its way inside the other, so the words that follow are placed around it
one piece has made its way inside the other, so the words that follow are placed around it

parts.note: malt is the grain brewers use
an ape is a monkey-like animal; the 's is a link meaning 'has'

explanation.surface: A naughty monkey has broken into the brewery's grain store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'got into' puts APE and R inside MALT. This archaic word comes from French for badly spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word for impudent or saucy, describing someone boldly disrespectful.

clue.text: Worry about offer of acetylene producer

indicators.note: one piece goes around the other, so the first word's letters surround the second

parts.note: care is worry or concern
a bid is an offer at an auction

explanation.surface: Concern about a bid for a gas maker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts CARE round BID.
explanation.definitionFit: Calcium compound of this kind reacts with water to give off acetylene gas, used in old lamps.

clue.text: Liqueur mixed in tea-set

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of these words are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A liqueur stirred into the tea service.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an aniseed-flavoured liqueur, a sweet drink.

clue.text: We hear that Alice's cat might prove explosive

indicators.note: signals the words are to be said out loud and judged by their sound

parts.note: Dinah is Alice's cat in Lewis Carroll's Alice books, followed by the word might

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that Alice's cat could cause a blast.
explanation.walkthrough: Alice's cat in Lewis Carroll is called Dinah; 'Dinah might' said out loud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a high explosive invented by Alfred Nobel, used in blasting.

clue.text: What Bunter did with these olives

definitions.text: What Bunter did with these olives

parts.words: What Bunter did with these olives
parts.note: Billy Bunter, the greedy schoolboy of Frank Richards's stories, gorged himself; olives can be filled with pimento

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's eating habits with a dish of olives.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the famously greedy fat boy of British school stories; the word means both what he did to himself and olives filled with a stuffing.
explanation.definitionFit: It means both overfed, as the glutton was, and filled with a savoury filling, as olives often are.

clue.text: Big Bertha's outside chance?

parts.note: Big Bertha was a huge German gun of the First World War that fired shells over great distances; an outside chance is an unlikely bet

explanation.surface: A large woman's slim hope of success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big Bertha' looks like a woman but is the giant German howitzer of 1914, whose fire was a distance shot; the phrase also means an unlikely bet.
explanation.definitionFit: A bet with little chance of winning, and also a shot fired over a great range.

clue.text: Willow has aspiration, but finds a problem in square leg

definitions.text: finds a problem in square leg

parts.note: aspiration is the breathed sound H
an osier is a kind of willow

explanation.surface: A cricket bat of willow, a hopeful player, and trouble at a fielding position.
explanation.walkthrough: Square leg is a cricket fielding position, but here it is a leg of odd shape that a stocking seller must fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in stockings and socks must fit legs of every shape, so an awkward one is his problem.

clue.text: Like property bond investment, not by the sea

definitions.meaning: money in a property bond is put into real estate, ground and buildings
away from the coast, in the interior of a country

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words it says where property bond money goes; as one word it means away from the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Money in property bonds is placed in real estate, and the interior of a country is away from the coast.

clue.text: Bow feet

parts.note: Bow is in the East End of London, home of Cockneys, whose rhyming slang has a phrase for feet

explanation.surface: Feet that are bowed, or bow-legged.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is an East End district of London; true Cockneys are born within sound of Bow bells, and their rhyming slang gives this phrase for feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Cockney rhyming slang for feet, rhyming 'meat' with 'feet'.

clue.text: Fine ones to include murder, de Quincey considered

definitions.text: Fine ones to include murder, de Quincey considered

parts.words: Fine ones to include murder, de Quincey considered
parts.note: Thomas De Quincey wrote the essay On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Branches of creative skill

explanation.surface: An essayist thought there were good reasons for including a killing.
explanation.walkthrough: De Quincey's satirical essay is titled On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts.
explanation.definitionFit: Painting, music and the like are creative disciplines, among which De Quincey ironically placed murder.

clue.text: The bird, or one encore?

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
bis is called out for an encore, Latin for twice

explanation.surface: A performer asks whether to give the bird or one more encore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bird' looks like jeering from an audience, but is a wading bird; 'bis' is a call for a repeat performance.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a long-billed wading bird, sacred in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Sporting dog detailed to make good …

indicators.note: with its tail cut off, so the last letter of the dog is removed

parts.note: a retriever is a gun dog that fetches game

explanation.surface: A gun dog trained to make good the shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' means de-tailed: the gun dog loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To recover or put right a bad situation is to rescue it.

clue.text: … in a cat-show where he is the judge?

definitions.text: … in a cat-show where he is the judge?

parts.words: … in a cat-show where he is the judge?
parts.note: the Isle of Man is famous for its tailless cats, and its judges have a special title

explanation.surface: A judge at a feline show.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'cat-show' is the Isle of Man, which shows off Manx cats; its judges carry a special title. The dots link it to the previous clue's dog.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of a judge on the Isle of Man.
